content: 1. The analysis of phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (pDST) data was conducted using both WHO-endorsed methods and other acceptable drug susceptibility testing (DST) methods. While the ALL dataset exhibited greater variability and noise in pDST results, its larger sample size was critical for identifying statistically significant relationships between genotypes and observed phenotypes. In cases where an isolate was tested multiple times using the same method but yielded inconsistent results, only concordant results were considered, and discordant results were excluded. This rule was also applied to binarized minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) data. 2. The bioinformatics pipeline for variant detection was adapted for public cloud infrastructure in the second edition of the analysis, but the core steps remained consistent with the first edition. PCR duplicates were removed using SAMtools, and when multiple sequencing runs were available for a single isolate, alignments were merged before genotyping. Genotyping was performed using FreeBayes for single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and small indels, and Delly for large deletions. Quality control included taxonomic assignment of aligned reads using Kraken, global sequencing metrics using SAMtools, and gene-specific sequencing metrics using Mosdepth. Only samples with a median sequencing depth greater than 15× and at least 95% of the reference genome covered at 20× were included in the analysis. 3. Variant annotation was performed independently of genotype identification, leveraging a relational database model. This allowed iterative extraction of new entries for annotation. Variants were normalized using BCFtools to ensure accurate annotation, and large deletions were annotated based on their genomic coordinates. For quality control, the median sequencing depth and genome coverage at various thresholds (15×, 20×, 25×, 30×) were recorded. Genes were considered missing if any nucleotide was sequenced fewer than 10 times. 4. The annotation process accounted for the effects of variants on genes and proteins, including missense, synonymous, and frameshift mutations. Variants were categorized based on their predicted effects, such as feature ablation for large deletions. The annotation of promoter variants required a modified reference sequence to account for linearized genome ends. A custom Python script was used to address issues with Human Genome Variation Society (HGVS) nomenclature and to normalize data for database insertion. 5. The catalog of mutations in the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex and their association with drug resistance was updated in the second edition. Candidate resistance genes were identified and categorized into tiers based on their relevance to drug resistance. Promoter and upstream regions of these genes were analyzed for their potential to alter downstream gene expression. Mutations in these regions were interpreted using nucleotide-based HGVS nomenclature. 6. Genetic changes with the same protein-altering effect were grouped and interpreted using protein-based HGVS nomenclature. Synonymous changes, which do not alter the protein, were treated individually and interpreted using nucleotide-based naming. Consecutive point mutations affecting the same codon were analyzed together, while those on different codons were treated separately. 7. The SOLO algorithm was employed to classify mutations as resistance-determining (aR), consistent with susceptibility (aS), or algorithmically uncertain (aU). Silent mutations were assumed to be neutral and masked during the analysis. Non-silent mutations found exclusively in phenotypically resistant isolates were classified as aR, while those found only in susceptible isolates were classified as aS. Mutations that could not be definitively classified were labeled as aU. 8. The SOLO algorithm was adapted from previous methods to identify individual mutations associated with resistance. It characterizes the effects of specific mutations in genes and promoters likely linked to phenotypic resistance expression. The algorithm's steps are outlined in detail, including the classification of mutations based on their occurrence in resistant or susceptible isolates. This explanation provides a detailed and professional summary of the methodologies and findings described in the original text, suitable for an expert audience.
